blocks.text: Second, that angels are signified by eagles is shown by the description of the four living creatures in Ezekiel and the Apocalypse ^{a)}, which we have explained elsewhere. Hence in Apoc. VIII, 13., where the common reading is Καὶ εἶδον, καὶ ἤκουσα ἑνὸς ἀγγέλου πετωμένου ἐν μεσουρανήματι [Kai eidon, kai ēkousa henos angelou petōmenou en mesouranēmati], instead of ἑνὸς ἀγγέλου [henos angelou] a Spanish manuscript of the highest quality, and following it the Complutensian and Plantin editions, have ἑνὸς ἀετοῦ [henos aetou]. So also Arethas in his Commentary on the Apocalypse, chapter 25. Nor did the Syriac and the Ethiopic read otherwise. Finally the old version has: I heard the voice of one eagle, flying through the midst of heaven, saying, etc. Both readings seem admissible: the one teaches that an angel appeared to John; the other, that this angel had the form of an eagle, which suits an angel exceedingly well because of its swiftness, strength and longevity, its τὸ ὀξυδερκὲς [to oxyderkes], its τὸ ὑψιπετὲς [to hypsipetes], and whatever else the eagle has in common with the angelic nature. [col. 184]

Third, the faithful seem to be signified by the name of eagles in the words of Christ, Matth. XXIV, 28. For wheresoever the carcass is, there will the eagles be gathered together. Of the many interpretations of this passage, the one I like best is that of Beza, by which this verse and the preceding one are connected with verse 26 as follows. If any should whisper that Christ is to be sought here or there, as though he were in hiding, do not believe it; for Christ will show himself openly, like lightning flashing from the east to the west and illuminating the whole world. And just as eagles fly at once to a carcass with wonderful keenness of scent, so in the end all the godly will likewise have to run together when they perceive the life-giving savour of the death of Christ. And not without reason are those who gather to Christ called eagles, since no one is united with him except one who feeds on his flesh and blood. Accordingly Jerome takes πτῶμα [ptōma], or carcass, to mean the passion of Christ. And Chrysostom, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, Homily 28, says that the body of Christ is called πτῶμα [ptōma] on account of his death. Applying this to the eucharistic communion of Christ, he adds that the faithful are called eagles, to show that he who approaches this body must strive towards the heights, and must have nothing in common with the earth, nor be drawn down to lower things and creep; but must always fly to higher things, gaze upon the sun of righteousness, and have the eye of the mind most sharp. Ἀετῶν γὰρ, οὐ κολοιῶν αὕτη ἡ τράπεζα [Aetōn gar, ou koloiōn hautē hē trapeza]· For this table is for eagles, not for jackdaws. In Luc. XVII, 37., where the Evangelist repeats the same saying of Christ, he has τὸ σῶμα [to sōma] instead of τὸ πτῶμα [to ptōma]. But it comes to the same thing. For [II, 769] Homer, Xenophon, Plutarch, Porphyry and other Greek writers commonly use τὸ σῶμα [to sōma] for a carcass.
